raw_comment: From the graph, I noticed that legacy applicants have a significantly higher admissions rate across the board (over twice the average rate). However, those wither higher parental income had a proportionally larger benefit: up to 7 times the average for the top 0.1%, compared to less than triple (already high) for non-legacy. This leaves several burning questions: among them, why are admissions so heavily skewed in favor of high-income, legacy applicants, and what steps can colleges take to reduce this (likely-systematic) bias?

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I can see that, for legacy applicants, applications of those with a family income rank of more than the 50th percentile essentially stays at a rate of 2.5 times as likely or more to be accepted. However, I'm noticing that non-legacies with an income rank of about 85% are under 1 times as likely to be accepted into an elite college. 

After analyzing the graph, I wonder how these admissions numbers will be impacted over the next several years. After the Supreme Court case in June that eliminated affirmative action in terms of college admissions on the grounds of things like race, I'm curious to see how this will extend to legacy statuses. Legacies aren't necessarily considered to be disadvantaged, but non-legacies may be, so it'll be interesting to see if legacy admissions rise or drop. 

This graph doesn't necessarily affect my immediate community very much, as I don't know anyone who was aiming to be accepted into a highly selective college. However, I do live in the general proximity of Rice University, which is a very selective college that likely exhibits admissions bias based on whether someone is a legacy and the income bracket that they are in. 

A headline that captures the graph's main idea might be "Application Distortion: Legacies vs. Everyone Else."

raw_comment: It was interesting to see how much a student's legacy can effect their acceptance rate, especially for students of parent's with higher incomes. For students of parents who have a mid to high income, legacy has a significant boost on their acceptance rates. I wonder why legacy is so important to these colleges. Parents and their children can differ significantly in character traits and personalities, which makes the idea of legacy a questionable way to admit students. If these colleges' goal is to attract and accept the most intelligent, talented, and skilled students, why is such an emphasis placed on legacy? It seems irresponsible of these colleges to accept based on legacy and unfair to the multitude of highly talented students who are rejected because they lack legacy.

raw_comment: I notice how legacy applicants with parents of higher income have a much higher chance of being accepted than that of someone "poorer" or a regular applicant. I wonder why it is more important to accept those whose parents have attended. Children aren't always the same as their parents. So why is there such a high chance for these higher income legacy applicants when there isn't a guarantee that they'll be similar. These legacy applicants could even be less academic than their parents. People who aren't legacy applicants though, such as myself, would have no where near as good of a shot without being a legacy applicant. This relates to me because as a Junior, I need to start looking for colleges. Not being a legacy applicant will affect my options greatly. A catchy headline for this could be: Status over Smarts?: Is being a legacy applicant more important than being academically smart?

raw_comment:
I noticed that for legacy applicants, they are 7x as likely to be admitted as opposed to applicants without legacy status, meaning that if an applicant had relatives with a history of attending a certain elite university such as Ivy Leagues, then they had a much higher chance of being accepted compared to an applicant who did not have any prior legacy status in their family. Also, the richer an applicant's parents' income rank was and the more upper class they were, the higher the chance they were to be admitted into an elite college, even under the scenario of students with the same test scores. 

I wonder why it's harder for applicants without legacy status to be admitted into the same university with the same scores as others who have family or are a apart of generations in their family that have a history of attending the elite college that they are currently applying too. While I do understand why generations of a family might wish to all attend the same prestigious school, I don't think it's fair to other applicants who work just as hard but are simply the first of their family to apply and wish to be admitted. However, I think that this current statistic very likely has to do with elite colleges wishing to keep their students "elite", and the fact that most legacy status applicants most likely come from wealthy families that are able to use connections and legacy history to their advantage.

raw_comment:
Apart from the stand-out jump in the admission rate for legacy applicants of the 99.9% income percentile, I found it interesting that the admissions rate was higher for non-legacy applicants of the <50% income percentile than it were for the 50-95% higher income percentile of those applying. Interestingly enough, the admissions rate for the same income brackets of legacy applicants do not follow this trend but rather continually get higher until reaching the extremes.
I wonder of what the admissions graph would look like if instead of using the income percentiles, the graph used fixed yearly salaries. According to what I saw in the bottom of the page, the 99 or 99.9 percentiles represented those with an income of 620k+, I would be interested to see how admissions rates change in the millions or tens/hundreds of millions range. I believe that this graph relates to Texas in the way that many students in this state, regardless of socioeconomic status, do not even apply to out-of-state colleges in the first place. Many students are happy to stick with applying with their regional legacy schools. As being from an immigrant family in Australia with no prior experiences of the American College system, I find it interesting regarding the state boundaries that many confine themselves to as the equivalent state/province boundaries in Australia are nowhere near as considered. For a title: "Elite Admissions Opportunities Impacted by Socio-Economic Status."

raw_comment:
It doesn't seem to have occurred to anyone that the most prestigious colleges are that way because of who they admit, and changing that is not going to give an advantage to those who were formerly not admitted, but will simply make these schools no longer prestigious.

That is, it is plausible that Harvard graduates are desirable because Harvard screens its applicants for desirability, not because of the education they get once they are there. It's a similar fallacy for all highly selective schools - if a school only allows in the best students (for whatever meaning of best you like), the school and it's teachers don't have to be any good, because the best students will excel regardless.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that legacy applicants had at least a doubled chance of being admitted and as parents' income rank increase so did the chance of admission. However, I noticed that the students whose parents had an income rank that was in the 50th rank or the middle rank had less of a chance of being admitted into the college.

2. I wonder why the legacy students' whose parents' income rank was in the middle of the rank or in the 50th rank had less of a chance of admission than the other legacy students with a lower or higher rank. Is this graph telling us that there is a possible abundance of legacy students with parents who are in the 50th income rank? Are people in the middle class experiencing some form of discrimination in the college process? Are we experiencing injustice or high demand?

3. This relates to my community in a great deal of ways. I am currently in high school and I plan to go to college. I am aware that college isn't the goal for all high school students, but I know that many students future plans include going to college. The people I surround myself with are mostly all academically motivated and are all trying very hard to make themselves appealing to colleges. We constantly strive to get good grades and fill our schedules with clubs and extra curriculars, while simultaneously keeping a social life. We are in high school after all.

4. ARE THE CHANCES OF BEING ADMITTED TO COLLEGE CONNECTED TO INCOME AND LEGACY?

I've found that, compared to typical students, Legacy students have an approximately twofold higher chance of being accepted into Elite universities. Additionally, I saw that the graph fell at the 85th percentile, but then it shot up to seven times higher acceptance rates. Why does the graph dip at about the 85th percentile, I wonder? In my neighborhood, I can relate to this because I'm a high school student approaching the age when students need to start thinking seriously about college. Resources like these assist students understand the admission rates to different universities.

"Knowledge is Liberty"

raw_comment:
I noticed that whether a person is a legacy or not makes a huge difference for upper middle class people. It is the hardest for this group to get in without legacy. The acceptance chance for the super wealthy is much higher regardless of legacy or not, though significantly higher with legacy.

I wonder why politicians are so concerned with the “unfair advantage“ that affirmative action gave when legacy acceptances are conveniently overlooked. “Shouldn’t we reward people based on their hard work and not luck of the draw?” A familiar argument used this past summer when affirmative action was overturned. But is being a person of color “luck of the draw”? Or is being a legacy, the majority of which are white, wealthy individuals not upholding systemic inequality?

I know a lot of legacy students and a lot of students who have been admitted into top 20s/Ivies on merit. Most of the legacy students I know are white, privileged, and relatively less accomplished than those who aren’t. In no way am I saying that legacy students are not as smart or as talented, but there is a clear favor towards these students.

“Lucky in Legacy: An Ivy’s four leaf clover”

raw_comment: This graph is highly relatable to my experience right now as a high school senior. It shows the advantage that legacy students have at Ivy League schools. raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   We had many terrific headlines this week.  Here are some student headlines that popped out while capturing the main idea of the graph:  “Inherited Admission to Elite Colleges” by Sky of Iowa; “College: The Legacy of a Rich Man’s World!” by Katherine of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, N.J.; two headlines from Perth Amboy High School in N.J. – “Nepotism at Ivy, Advantages Not Even Money Could Buy!” by Santiago and “The Legacy Continues, The Gap Widens” by Emily; “"Are You Rich? Are You a Legacy? Welcome to Harvard!" by Alyson Lu of California; 
"Who's Applying: You or Your Parents?" by Texas of Pewaukee High School in Wis. and SIX headlines from Michigan:  "Data Shows Elite Colleges Who Preach ‘Equity’ Still Favor Legacies and the Upper Class" by Seth of Traverse City West Senior High School; “No Legacy, No Money, No Luck: Bias in College Admissions” by Molly and “Ivy League or Legacy League” by Cameron, both of Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich.;  “College Admissions Skewed: The Effects of Income and Legacy” by Maxwell of Richland, Mich.; “What Are Colleges Really Looking for in an Application: Rich Legacy Parents!” by Aidan of Mich. and “Wealth and Legacy: Is This Mainly What Admissions Care About?” by Henry of Mich.

raw_comment:
I noticed that legacy applicants had more than double the advantage of being admitted into college compared to non-legacy students. I also noticed that up until the 99.9 percentile, the graph stays kind of flat, but then it suddenly grows for both legacy and non-legacy students. The 99.9 percentile of legacy applicants have more than 6x the advantage compared to the average. Still, the 99.9 percentile of non-legacy applicants has around the same advantage or less than the poorer legacy applicants. 

I wonder why they value legacy students more than even the rich non-legacy students. I also wonder how different the admission process is for non-legacy, legacy, rich, and poor. 

It relates to me because a lot of people think that whether you go to college or not is a very important determinant of your future. As someone who wants to go to college, seeing these kinds of statistics can be discouraging, as you know someone else will be considered first in line matter what you do, especially if you are not a legacy applicant. 
“Elite Colleges Have Preferences”

raw_comment:
"There ARE Advantages in Elite College Admissions!"

Students whose parents' incomes are in the top 5% are far more likely to be admitted into a prestigious university.  Interestingly, students whose parents are in the 70-95th percentile get accepted less frequently.  Additionally, legacy applicants are far more likely to be admitted.  I wonder why universities care so much about the students' wealth in the admission process.  This means that students from low-income households and/or are first-generation college students are at a disadvantage.  Some universities are becoming need-blind and offering resources for first-generation college students to excel after high school.

raw_comment: The graph depicts how being a legacy affects an applicant's chances of being accepted into a school. For more elite schools, the familial ties a student has to a school could be the largest factor in their application, boosting their chances about 7x. Nearly all students at the most prestigious universities are legacy students. This affects me because I am in the college admissions process. My chances of being admitted to an Ivy League are very low because I am not a legacy at any of them. I wonder why this kind of bias is still allowed in the decision process. There have been legislations passed in the last few years that have taken race, economic, and standardized testing bias out of the process. The fact that legacy consideration is still used seems unethical. A possible headline could be "How are your chances of getting into Harvard?"

raw_comment:
This graph compares students with the same test scores and how their chances of being admitted to elite colleges can fluctuate based on their legacy status and their parent's income rank. It is clear from this graph that in every income rank, legacy status helps boost admission. I find it insane that very wealthy people with legacy status are 7x more likely to get into a school than a poorer person without status who worked just as hard to get the same scores. I wonder why there is such a bias in college admissions. One reason for this bias is that wealthy families may donate a lot of money to the school which could put applicants at an advantage. However, one would assume that by having all this wealth, one already has an advantage in life. Therefore, giving a wealthy and a poor person who both have legacy status and have the same scores unequal opportunities is solidifying those societal norms. Also the poor students not getting into these elite colleges because they are put at an inherent disadvantage when applying, it is further hindering their opportunities in life. I wonder if giving out financial aid is one of the reasons that poorer students who have the same credentials as wealthy students have a less likely chance of getting into a school. I know that financial aid is limited. This affects me because I will be applying to colleges soon. Some schools are doing away with legacy status, so I am not sure how much this graph will affect me. 
"Legacy Boost= Bias"

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph shows how much of an advantage wealthy legacy children have for getting into the country's top "prestigious" colleges. I notice that your parent's income has a big pull on your chances of acceptance. I wonder if schools will start to defer or reject more legacy to make it more fair for other applicants who are more deserving. This relates to me and my community because many of my friends including myself our top schools were schools our siblings or parents had attended. I have grown very familiar with this process over the past few months as a senior in high school. I have started to hear of a lot more legacies getting deferred in the early action applicant pool and being moved to regular decisions. 
Headline:
Is the college application process as fair as we think??

raw_comment:
I noticed that legacy applicants have a significant advantage in the college admissions process over people applying without a legacy status to elite colleges. However, I also noticed that it is 7 times more likely that a legacy applicant to an elite college would be admitted if their parents’ income is higher than the 90th percentile. Additionally, I find it interesting that there is a dip in the graph for applicants without a legacy status in which the parents are around the 70th percentile in income. This is intriguing because parents with a relatively low income (in the “poorer” income rank) were two times as likely to be admitted. With this, I noticed and wondered why the “poorer” and “richer” extreme income rank almost reached the same likelihood of admittance for non-legacy applicants. Furthermore, I wonder how the graph would appear individually for each of the elite colleges (which elite college favors more legacies overall?). The graph relates to my community because as a senior, I along with many of my classmates are going through the college admissions process. This makes me wonder how money and legacies will affect my classmates’ admissions to certain colleges. 

“Are Elite Colleges Truly for Elite Students or the Elite?”

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a legacy boost in elite colleges, meaning that if a parent or sibling goes there you have a much higher chance of getting into that college. I noticed that students who are wealthier, have a greater chance of getting admitted as well. 
I wonder why having a parent or sibling that previously went to that college makes a effect on whether or not a student gets admitted or not, because shouldn’t the college be focusing on you, not others? 
This relates to me and my community, because I am currently a senior making college decisions, and my chances may be lower or higher than other people just based on a family legacy. 
What’s going on in this graph is that it is showing the effects of how legacy and wealth contribute to one’s chance of being admitted into college. A catchy headline would be: If You Have A Legacy, it is Your Legacy To Come To College!

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that legacy applications were admitted at a considerably higher rate than non-legacy applicants, irrespective of income. Additionally, the chance of admission for students with the greatest income is little over two times, which is insignificant when compared to legacy students who have a parent income rate of 99.9.
2. I wonder about the role that money plays in the school's admissions process. Is there evidence of favoritism in the amount of legacy students being admitted? What distinguishes legacy students from non-legacy students as superior applicants? Does the admission of legacy students depend on the actions of their alumni at these schools?
3. This is relevant to me and my community because I'm from an urban area, which means that many of my peers and classmates have not had the same luck as me in being legacy students or having parents who were alumni. As a result, admission is even more difficult for those who are already at a disadvantage due to circumstances beyond their control.
4. Rags To Riches, Is Favoritism Ending Fair Chances?

raw_comment:
1. Legacy applicants have an advantage at some elite colleges than those without legacy status. Overall, students whose parents are in the top 5% of income rank have a much higher chance of admission.
2. I wonder why there is a dip for non-legacy applicants between 75-90%.Is it legal to admit based off financial or legacy status? Is this true for non-elite colleges.

4. "Who's applying: you or your parents?"

raw_comment:
I noticed that legacy students of all income rankings tend to see significantly higher admission rates than non legacy students. To a certain extent, income also seems to be a determining factor in admission rates. Students with family incomes ranking in the top 10% are much more likely to be admitted than those in the bottom 10%. 

The fact that students are more likely to be admitted when their family income is higher is interesting. Many colleges claim to be need-blind when looking at college applications, so the data has to be due to other factors possibly influenced by higher income. Students with more resources have easier access to information, tutors, or other outside assistance. These resources are likely to positively impact their academic performance and college applications. However, students with less resources end up disadvantaged in comparison to these students.

This graph sheds light on how a student’s family background — something they have no control over — can impact their lives. A student whose family has a higher income and more access to resources will typically end up more successful than one with a lower income. As a community, students with less access to resources needed for academic excellence need to be addressed. If we can address this issue, we can reduce the disparity between legacy and non-legacy, or high-income and low-income.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

The higher income you have the more likely you are to be admitted. 

Legacy students have a much higher acceptance. 

2. What do you wonder?

Why does legacy matter? 

How has this changed overtime?
Does this graph apply to other prestigious universities that aren't ivy Leagues?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

As someone who is in the process of college applications, it highlights the unequal circumstances that admit students. These circumstances, income and legacy, are not things that people choose or do but are born into. This makes it impossible for other students to reach this same amount of admissions based on choice and decision alone. 4) Did you get accepted into college or are you just a legacy?

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that legacy applications were admitted at a considerably higher rate than non-legacy applicants, irrespective of income. Additionally, the chance of admission for students with the greatest income is little over two times, which is insignificant when compared to legacy students who have a parent income rate of 99.9.
2. I wonder about the role that money plays in the school's admissions process. Is there evidence of favoritism in the amount of legacy students being admitted? What distinguishes legacy students from non-legacy students as superior applicants? Does the admission of legacy students depend on the actions of their alumni at these schools?
3. This is relevant to me and my community because I'm from an urban area, which means that many of my peers and classmates have not had the same luck as me in being legacy students or having parents who were alumni. As a result, admission is even more difficult for those who are already at a disadvantage due to circumstances beyond their control.
4. Rags To Riches, Is Favoritism Ending Fair Chances?

raw_comment:
This graph depicts the likelihood of admissions advantages at some colleges compared to those with the same test scores and a legacy advantage. I noticed how a legacy student with wealthier parents who are in the top 0.1% of income would be 7x more likely to be admitted into a school compared to a less wealthy student. That definitely must annoy students trying to get into an elite college. I also noticed that regardless of income, legacy applicants were admitted significantly higher than those without legacy status. I noticed that students who have a legacy advantage are more wealthy compared to those without a legacy advantage. I wonder how this could be and why there is a lesser legacy for students with low income. Maybe it could be because the wealthier applicants can afford high tuition costs and donate money to the elite college whereas the low-income ones would struggle and would request financial aid.  I wonder how income and legacy advantages affect a student getting into an elite college in the admission process. Like if you request financial aid are you more likely to be deferred or rejected? This affects me and my community because I am a sophomore who is starting to research college so next year I will be applying and looking at schools. Also, I have 2 older sisters who have applied to colleges without a legacy advantage and got in. But my family friend with a legacy advantage for Villanova as her uncle went there, got differed.

raw_comment:
The graph depicts the admissions rate for students with the same test scores, and how they vary based on legacy and parent's income. Legacy applicants are much more likely to be admitted. For income, the general trend seems to be that the more an applicant's parents make, the better chance they have. 
However, there is one anomaly that I noticed. For those who are not legacies, the admittance rate goes down before going back up at around the 90th percentile. I'm not sure why this is. Maybe universities try to accept students who are either extremely wealthy or poor. 
As someone who is looking to go to college, I don't want to be impaired by something I can't control, such as how much money my parents make. This inequality affects every students striving to get a higher education by promoting those who already have an advantage.

raw_comment:
What I notice in this graph is how students applying to colleges automatically get an advantage with being a legacy, but meanwhile, it shows how the more money a family makes the higher chances they have of getting into a harder school. Also how the families who are the richest and have the best legacy connections tend to have the absolute best chances of getting in over everyone else even if they have the same test scores. What I wonder is how having a lot of money and being a legacy have changed over the course of history. Did it used to always be this way? This affects my community because I was recently applying to colleges a few months ago and I was wondering how all of these factors could affect my application process as well. What is going on in this graph is it is trying to depict how parents who have higher incomes and students who have a legacy with the school, tend to be accepted over other students with similar test scores.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
The legacy boost isn’t even as you move across the line of the income status (the boost for 70th is much higher than 10th, but a lot lower than 99th) 
For those in the top 10% of wealth, if they are a legacy, their chances of being accepted skyrocket, especially compared to those who aren’t legacy and are in the bottom 70-80%. 

2. What do you wonder?
What test was used?
What were the scores? 
Why did they choose only these schools? 
Did they account for the fact that some schools only removed their legacy policy in the later dates of the range of which they studied, which would skew the data? 
It’s highly unlikely that test scores are the only thing that influences admission, so what other variables could be impacting admission, such as their essay, resume, etc.? 

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
Since I am a senior and I am applying to college, for elite colleges, I am often competing with applicants who have legacy. This makes it harder for me to get into the colleges that I want because those with legacy have a higher chance of getting in, which then lowers my own chance of acceptance. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
Elitism of Elite Schools
Daddy's Money gets you in the Ivy League

raw_comment:
I notice that the estimated legacy boost is much higher for the top 0.1%-- they are 7 times as likely to be admitted. I also notice that the upper middle class (75-90th income rank) has a lower than average admission rate. The admissions rate tends to be higher than average for poorer and richer families.

I wonder when admission rates became so much higher for legacy students; did the trend start when admissions became more selective? I also wonder why the upper middle class is disadvantaged in college admissions. Is there anything being done to mitigate the legacy boost? Also, do the top  0.1% also fare better because they have more money to invest in extracurriculars and tutoring?

This relates to me and my community because I will enter college soon. Since my classmates and I will be competing against legacy students who have a much higher likelihood of getting into selective schools, this may hurt our chances at admissions.

This graph shows the disparate admission rates at elite colleges for legacy and nonlegacy students, as well as between the rich and the poor.

"The Golden Touch: College Admissions"

1. I noticed that regardless of income, legacy applicants were admitted significantly higher than those without legacy status. Furthermore, even with the highest income the likelihood of students being admitted is slightly over 2x which pales in comparison to legacy students with a 99.9 parent income rate.
2. I wonder how income factors into the school's decisions as to who is admitted and who isn't. Does the number of legacy students being admitted suggest nepotism? What makes legacy students better applicants than non-legacy students? Does it matter what the alumni did at these schools for the legacy students to get admitted?
3. This relates to me and my community as being from an urban community it means that a number of my classmates/peers have not had the same fortune of being legacy students/having parents that were alumni thus making admission that much harder for those already at a disadvantage for something completely out of their control (with parental/guardian income also being completely out of these students control). 
4. Nepotism at Ivy, Advantages Not Even Money Could Buy!

raw_comment:
This graph shows the relationship between elite colleges and their tendency to choose applicants based on economic status and family legacy. The black line (legacy applicants) is significantly higher than the gray line (non-legacy applicants), indicating that elite schools favor legacy. Legacy applicants appear to automatically have double the chance of acceptance. It also is apparent that both types of applicants have a spiked chance of getting into an elite college when their parent’s income surpasses the 90th percentile. One thing that stood out to me was that applicants without legacy status who fall into the middle-class range have less of a chance of getting into an elite college versus an applicant with poorer or richer incomes. Do colleges discriminate against middle-class applicants because they are not rich enough to generate a lot of money but not poor enough to even out their statistics in appearing to be a school that caters to all financial statuses? This relates to me because as a current senior applying to college, I have had to witness students get into colleges just because of their legacy status and or because their parents have a higher income. Even though we may have the same statistics, colleges will always choose the legacy/richer applicant. This has hurt all students, not just me, and our disadvantage when it comes to being a middle class without legacy status when applying to elite colleges. 

“College: The Legacy of a Rich Man’s World!”

The next graph will be released by Friday, February 2 with live moderation on Wednesday, February 7.  The topic – 2023 global temperatures.

raw_comment:
1. I notice the extreme boost in odds of admission for legacy applicants and for some reason a boost for kids with parts in the top 1-5%. I also notice there isn’t my change based on income at any point below the top 5%. Finally I notice that strangely income has a much greater effect for legacy applicants than it does for normal applicants. 
2. I wonder why there is such a difference between normal and legacy applicants as you would expect the college to accept the best applicants and not those with parents who went there previously. I also wonder how income can affect admissions so greatly, I wonder if it is because they have more support to build a better application or if it's actually part of the admissions calculations. Finally I wonder why income hurts your chances as a normal applicant (until top 5ish percent) though it boosts your chances as a legacy applicant. 
3. Admission to college is very important to me and to many other students in my community. The majority of us are not legacy applicants and if there is truly this great disadvantage that comes with this fact it would greatly damage the hopes of many students in my district. Additionally my district is very split on parents' financial status and truly this shouldn’t be affecting admissions as I don’t think the most supported kids are very often the smartest or hardest working students. 
4. College Admissions Skewed: The Effects of Income and Legacy

raw_comment:
1. I notice the extreme boost in odds of admission for legacy applicants and for some reason a boost for kids with parts in the top 1-5%. I also notice there isn’t my change based on income at any point below the top 5%. Finally I notice that strangely income has a much greater effect for legacy applicants than it does for normal applicants. 
2. I wonder why there is such a difference between normal and legacy applicants as you would expect the college to accept the best applicants and not those with parents who went there previously. I also wonder how income can affect admissions so greatly, I wonder if it is because they have more support to build a better application or if it's actually part of the admissions calculations. Finally I wonder why income hurts your chances as a normal applicant (until top 5ish percent) though it boosts your chances as a legacy applicant. 
3. Admission to college is very important to me and to many other students in my community. The majority of us are not legacy applicants and if there is truly this great disadvantage that comes with this fact it would greatly damage the hopes of many students in my district. Additionally my district is very split on parents' financial status and truly this shouldn’t be affecting admissions as I don’t think the most supported kids are very often the smartest or hardest working students. 
4. College Admissions Skewed: The Effects of Income and Legacy

As well as any applicants with legacy's have up to 7 times the chance of getting accepted into college. raw_comment:
1. What I notice is that the higher the student's parent income is, the more likely they are to get accepted to college, while people who have a lower income are less likely to be accepted to college. I also recognize how leacy helps students get accepted, as for those who do not have it, they get under the average admission rate.
2. I wonder how far does having a higher income take you. For instance, if you are rich but you do not meet the college requirements, will they still accept you for your income as if you have a lower income but you meet all the requirements?
3. This is relevant to my community because it contributes to social inequality by limiting educational opportunities for those who have a lower income. It's not fair that just because you have a higher income, you mostly get accepted to college compared to someone who struggles financially. This creates an environment where success is tied to a higher income.
4. "The Secret to Instant Admission Revealed!"

raw_comment:
It appears that as Parents’ income rank rises, so does the estimated legacy boost. Also, up until roughly the 85th percentile for Parents’ income rank, there is a decrease in the likelihood to be admitted, whereas there is on average a consistent likelihood to be admitted after the legacy boost. Finally, after the 85th percentile, there is an increase in admission likelihood for both students with and without the legacy boost, although there is a more drastic increase for those with the legacy boost.
I wonder why the likelihood of admittance for legacy applicants remains close to constant for most of the graph. Why does the likelihood of admittance drop so drastically for non-legacy applicants around the 70th Parent’s income rank?
For people from my community, this shows that those with parents who graduated from selective schools are more likely to be admitted than those whose parents did not graduate from a selective school. We could also generalize this to more than just the twelve selective schools and say that applicants are more likely to be admitted to a school if their parents graduated from there. 
“Systemic generational bias in higher education”

raw_comment:
1) I've seen that wealthier students are more likely to get into college. I've also noticed that students with legacies have a far better chance of getting accepted. It's not morally right but a common trend shown in this graph.

2) I'm curious if you can still get in on Legacy despite not being wealthy, or if it will reduce your chances. Do universities allow more wealthy students because they can repay their tuition faster than those who take out loans? I wonder if someone with superior grades or a more remarkable resume can overcome a  family legacy.

3) This affects me and my community since I know several students who will be the first in their families to attend college. My town isn't exactly wealthy, so how will they achieve their goal if legacies are preferred? My community will have a harder time if rates continue to rise at the same rate as the expected legacy increase. 

4) Did you get accepted into college or are you just a legacy?

1.Once the parents' income rank reached the 99th percentile, there was a major jump in admissions advantage. The first jump in estimated boost begins around the 70th income rank percentile for both legacy and non-legacy applicants. Around the 50th and 80th percentile advantage for students with and without legacy status goes down. 

2.I wonder what caused a drop in admission advantages for both groups of students around the 50th and 80th percentiles.

3.In my high school, every year students apply to all different kinds of colleges and universities. It is both interesting and tiresome to see that just because of a student's income and legacy status, they might have a better chance of getting into college. It is sad that students that have scores and resumes on the same level may get rejected from certain colleges and universities because of things that they cannot control.

4.Should Legacies Be the Only Ones to Leave a Legacy?

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
-The applicants with parents on the wealthier end of the spectrum who are not legacies are less likely to get accepted then poorer non-legacy applicants. 
-People with rich, alumni parents are the most likely to be accepted into the university. 
-Where the rich alumni admissions spike, the rich non-alumni applicant admissions drop. 

What do you wonder? 
-Why are these students applying? What is their reasoning behind their applications? 

What’s the relation? 
Both of my parents are alumnis at Michigan State University. It thus follows that I’ve grown up going to campus- I love it up there, however that doesn’t mean that I want to go there. However, a lot of people want (or expect) me to go there because of my parents. I wonder then, what the pressure on the legacies is. Perhaps the Ivy Leagues favor legacies. But, could it also be that a lot of the legacies applying there apply because they are legacies? 

Title: 
A Legacy of Parental Pressure

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

This graph demonstrates the likelihood of acceptance to an elitist college by comparing factors including wealth and whether the student is a legacy, all with the same test scores. It shows that being a legacy immediately gives one an advantage no matter their current social status but also that as they become wealthier their chances increase with the top 0.1% being 7 times more likely to be accepted.

I wonder why there are a few dips in the graph, especially right around the 0.5% middle class and the people right before the top 0.1%. What makes them less likely to be accepted?

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

This impacts me and my community because me and my classmates are currently applying to college. It's important that we understand the hidden factors that inflounce our acceptance apart from our test scores. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

Is being a legacy no longer a promise of acceptance? 

Top 0.1% fueling their own success, is being wealthy the real deciding factor in college acceptances?

raw_comment:
1. According to the graph, I notice that legacy applicants with a wealthier background overall have a greater opportunity of being admitted into elite colleges. Whereas those with no legacy and a poorer status have a significantly lower possibility of being admitted into these elite colleges. In the graph, as parents' income rank continues to increase, applicants with a legacy can be up to 7x more likely to be admitted to elite colleges compared to those who have no benefits and no legacy which only fall into a little more than 2x probability of being admitted.
2. Even though all students had the same test scores, I wonder why colleges choose to accept those with an overall financially stable background rather than giving an equal opportunity to all students. Is this due to colleges believing that wealthier students will be able to pay off any college debt compared to poorer students?
3. This relates to me and my community because being that high schoolers are preparing to take on important decisions when choosing their dream colleges, these aspects that colleges are looking at can affect the acceptance rate of their admissions being accepted. 
4. Step 1:Money, Step 2:A legacy, Great, Welcome to college!

raw_comment:
I notice that the wealthier you and your family are, the higher chance you have of getting into an Ivy League college. This is shown in the graph when the top 0.1% is 7x more likely to get into an Ivy League college compared to others.

I wonder whether Ivy League colleges are more focused on the wealth and status of a student rather than their academic successes and abilities. It seems like these schools prefer and favor the richer and wealthier students so that makes me question if these schools aren't simply for the smartest, but for the wealthiest.

This relates to me and my community because many people in my community dream of attending an Ivy League school. But since they don't have the status that these schools favor, their chances are very low and require nothing short of a miracle to even have a chance to attend these schools.

Is Your Social Status Worthy Enough For the Ivy Leagues?

raw_comment:
I notice that when it comes to comparing students with the same test scores and figuring out who to admit to an elite college, legacy applicants have a much better chance of getting admitted. But, when money is added to the picture, non-legacy applicants that come from poorer families have a higher chance of being admitted than wealthy non-legacy applicants.This trend is shown throughout with the top 0.1% being 7x more likely to get in than someone with comparing attributes but no legacy.

I wonder why the colleges pay attention to the students' background and income more than their test scores. If a non-legacy student had a higher test score than a legacy student would it convince the colleges to admit them over the legacy student?

This relates to me and my community because as a high schooler, we are preparing to enter college and pursue a career meaning people my age or older have to take in consideration of these details, we must be aware of our possibilities and take advantage of what we can. 


Legacy Status Is The Leeway to College! How Is This Fair To Others!

Wealthy in Knowledge or Wealthy in Reputation?

raw_comment:
1) Without legacy status, I've seen that your chances of getting admitted are lower the more money your parents make, unless you are among the top 0.1%.  However, students with legacy status do not fully follow the trend.  The admittance rate for legacy status students often rises with the income of their parents; if you are among the top 0.1%, your chances are nearly doubled.
2)I wonder why the admissions process to Ivy League colleges is so competitive; the likelihood of being accepted increases dramatically with income. I believe this is the case because elite universities want wealthy students, and wealthy parents will undoubtedly pay them a lot of cash to get their inferior kids into such esteemed institutions. I believe that institutions have the conceited right to raise tuition and elevate their status when so-called "elites" enroll in Ivy League schools.
3)This is relevant to my town as a large number of individuals there are preparing to enter college, and if this is taken into account when making admissions decisions, it might lead to issues with college admittance.
4) "Dear College Am I Rich Enough For You"

raw_comment:
1)
I notice that there's about a 2x boost for legacies of any kind, and that it stays constantly above the non-legacy line. I also notice that the extremely wealthy legacies, ie; the 0.1 percentile are nearly 7x more likely to be accepted. Considering that elite colleges have an acceptance rate of about 3.3% to 7.3%, the acceptance rate for rich legacies is about 23.1% to 51.1%. This is important because traditionally, people who go to elite colleges are more likely to be rich in the future. The boost given to wealthy people and to legacies is meant to keep the class divide obvious and the school selective. 
 
2)
I wonder if this legacy boost exists in every single college. What would happen if each college had an individual graph plotting the difference between legacy and non-legacy? Does this bias go on to affect other things at the college, like grades, clubs, etc? Why is there a dip in the graph at around 50th and below the 90th?  What is it about these top 0.1 percentile legacies that makes colleges so incredibly drawn to them?

3)
This relates to my and my community because I am planning to go to college one day, and being a middle class non-legacy, it feels discouraging to apply to Ivy League and other elite schools. And even if I were to get accepted into these schools, many of the people I would be attending with would also be extremely wealthy, leading to a difference in experience and in values. 

4)
"Are You Rich? Are You a Legacy? Welcome to Harvard!"

raw_comment:
I notice that according to the graph the children who come from the top 0.1% of wealth in America are 7 times more likely to be admitted in elite colleges.  I wonder if the mode for the poor population of students are targeted by colleges or if its just by chance. For the poor population the 30th percentile mark has the highest chance to be admitted to a college. The chance proceeds to decline before and after that percentile only ascending again when it goes to the 70th percentile. This relates to me and my community because many people in Perth Amboy come from the lower financial side. It is very discouraging to realize that even though my peers and I are very educated and intelligent our application to elite colleges are looked differently than of an application that comes from wealth. 
Colleges Care About your $$$$

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The very first thing I noticed while looking at the graph is how much more likely legacy students are to be admitted into college. There is a significant trend indicating how legacy students are far more likely to be admitted into ivy league colleges. The second thing I noticed is how rich-non legacy kids are less likely to be admitted compared to poor-non legacy students. The third thing I notice is how the percentage of rich-legacy students have the biggest advantage in getting into the Ivy League.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the admission officials care so much about legacy. Does it increase profit? I also wonder why more wealthy kids who have no legacy have less of a chance of being admitted into college. 

How does this affect me and my community?
My classmates and I are going to be starting the college process very shortly and knowing the chances with legacy and whatnot can be a huge factor. It makes many students ask the question- “do I have less of a chance of getting into a college because I have no legacy and no wealth”? It seems to create an unfair advantage to me and my community which is very concerning to some.

Headline
Wealth and legacy- is this mainly what admissions care about?

raw_comment:
What do you notice? One thing I noticed was that the richer you are with legacy parents the more likely to get in. Essentially to have a decent shot at getting into elite colleges you need to have immense privilege. 

What do you wonder? One thing I wonder is why the poorer students are, the higher chance they have of getting in compared to wealthier non-legacy students, as well as how much of a role the “trauma essay” plays in this difference. 

How does this relate to you and your community? As someone who will apply to college soon, it makes me realize just how complicated and competitive college admissions can be. Your station in life is a huge factor in the colleges you can or can’t go to, something prevalent in students' and parents' minds as applications start and deadlines roll in.

Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea. “Ivy Leagues: Elite Schools or Elitists?”

raw_comment:
1) I notice that legacy students have a greater chance overall of being admitted into elite schools than students without the status. After the 50th percentile, while the chances to get admitted for legacy students went up, it had gone down for students without the status. Students without the status chances of being admitted had decreased the richer their families were, even going below average until after the 90th percentile of parents' income rank as their chances rose again. 

2) Why is the legacy status valued more? Why did the chance of being admitted decrease so much for normal students between the 70th and after the 90th percentile of parents' income? How many students hold the legacy status in these schools?

3) As many people are applying to college, it seems rather unfair that they'll have fewer chances of being admitted if they don't have the legacy status. As applying to elite schools is already very competitive, it is a great disadvantage as normal students also do the hard work getting the same grades, yet have less chances of getting in. When in all ways, students with legacy status always have the benefit of the doubt if they'll get in or not.

4) The College Admission Game: Perks of Being Legacy Status

raw_comment:
I notice that there is an obvious correlation between parents’ income and the likelihood of getting into an Ivy League. Also, when your parents or another close relative went to that college, the chances of getting accepted are about doubled for every income level. Additionally, I notice a subtle increase in acceptance rates at the low end of the income spectrum, presumably because of financial aid.

I wonder why the Ivy League college system is like this; your chances of getting in are significantly larger if you’re extremely wealthy. I think it’s because the colleges like to have rich people attending their schools and the rich surely pay them a large amount of under-the-table money to get their sub-par children into such renowned schools. I think when so-called “elites” attend the Ivy Leagues, colleges then have the self-adorned right to raise tuition and make their school more prestigious.

This relates to me because I am a high school junior looking to go to a good college and I am curious about acceptance rates vs. income and other factors, such as the legacy status. My entire community is mostly just my school and a small town, so I suppose many of the people in my community (at least those whom I regularly interact with) would be concerned about similar issues within the elite college community.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
When it comes to comparing students with the same test scores and figuring out who to admit to an elite college, legacy applicants have a much better chance of getting admitted. But, when money is added to the picture, non-legacy applicants that come from poorer families have a higher chance of being admitted than wealthy non-legacy applicants.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why the colleges pay attention to the students' background and income more than their test scores. If a non-legacy student had a higher test score than a legacy student would it convince the colleges to admit them over the legacy student?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me because I am currently in high school and I will start preparing for college some time next year, and if I'm not a legacy student, or a poor non-legacy student, but I still get good test scores, will I have a good chance of getting admitted?

raw_comment:
I noticed that as your parent's income rank increases, the better chance you have at getting accepted. I also noticed that the legacy applicants have more than double the shot at getting in, rather than the non-legacy students. Taking another look at the 90th rank and beyond, we see that there is a dip in acceptance and then a 7x increase. I know that people at either end of the graph have greater chances of attending because of diversity applicants and federal grant applicants, while juxtaposing that idea, the elite rich love to seperate themselves from others so the right side of the graph is not unexpected. 
I wonder if other colleges at local and community levels would have similar looking graphs? What about on the international level? I wonder if we did this survey again in 10 years would we yield the same results? 
This impacts my community because my friends and I are not legacies and yet some of them try so much harder, it's hard to know that students would be chosen over them just based on famialial history. 
"Colleges are the new alabama, Keeping it in the family"

We notice that students who are legacy applicants of elite colleges have a significantly higher chance of being admitted into the college than those without legacy status. We also notice that applicants are more likely to be admitted if their parents' income rank is among the highest overall.

We wonder why is the Estimated Legacy Boost much higher between richer people who are legacy applicants and who aren't versus between poorer people who are legacy applicants and who aren't?

This relates to our community because in our high school, majority of the students come from middle-class income families and could have a chance at being accepted into elite colleges. The distribution of admission rates shows that elite colleges have hidden preferences over legacy students versus non legacy students, as well as richer families being more accepted than poorer families. Since we come from middle-class families, we should be more unsure about our chances of admission if we apply to an elite college, especially that we may not have a legacy boost to.

raw_comment:
I noticed that elite colleges pay attention to a whole lot more than your grades and test scores. They look at how rich your parents are or how poor. Also, they look at if they have gone to their school or any elite school before. Depending on those results you may be more or less likely to be accepted. 

I wonder why they base their decisions based off of parental income and where their parents went. What does that do with the current kid? Are we really just going to trash his application based off of a background he or she has absolutely no control over?

This relates heavily to me because I am a student with grades applicable to elite colleges and schools and knowing that they are going to base my acceptance based on our income amount and where my parents went to school can be a very important thing to consider. Knowing I am already at a disadvantage because of that makes me realize just how much harder I and many other students in the same situation have to work to get ahead of these other more privileged students.

Elite Schools Throwing Away Elite Applicants for Family Legacies.

raw_comment:
I noticed that overall, regardless of income, legacy applicants have a much better chance of getting into elite colleges. However, non-legacy applicants who come from poorer families have a better chance than non-legacy applicants who come from wealthier families except for the very rich. The very rich non-legacy applicants have the best chance overall out of the non-legacy applicants.
I wonder if the college looks at the students' backgrounds. Is this why the legacy applicants have a better chance? Would having higher test scores than a legacy applicant still put you at a disadvantage? How much does income really compare to legacy status?
This relates to me because I am a high school student who is going to be applying to colleges soon. I want to know how much income and legacy will really affect my chances at different colleges. This relates to my community because my friends are going to have to go through the exact same process. It will be interesting to see how the applications and results shake-up when it is all finished.
Are Colleges Picking Favorites?

raw_comment:
I noticed that there is a significant gap between the legacy boost and the estimated advantage without the legacy boost. Even without the legacy boost the graph shows that when you are in the 99.9 percentile of your parents' income rank, you are still around 3x more likely to be accepted into an IV school. 

I wonder if students ever have an issue with this and sometimes feel that they just got into these schools because of their parents. I feel like I would feel that I didn't deserve to be there and I would want to get into the school on my own. I also wonder if the parents will notice this and begin to do something about it or if they just do not care enough. 

This relates to me because I will be soon applying to colleges and it is interesting to learn more about statistics. It is interesting to learn that my community is middle-upper class and that diminishes our chances of getting into an IV league school. It is kind of frustrating to learn that income is a part of being accepted into college, while it should be about your education levels and many other things not including your parents' income. 

What Do Colleges Really Think About When Looking At Applications? Is it Rigged?

raw_comment:
Notice:
Admission spikes for the top 0.1% regardless of a student's legacy status. 
For poorer students, the admission gap between legacy and non-legacy applicants is fairly stable. For applicants above the fiftieth percentile, legacy students have a much higher advantage. 
Admittance of non-legacy students dips after the 70th percentile and spikes again around 99.
Non-legacy students have the best admittance if either above the 90th percentile or below the 50th: upper/middle-class students don't have great chances unless legacy. probably because neither in need of financial aid nor willing/able to fund programs. 
Wonder: 
Other than test scores, legacy status, and parental income, what factors are considered? How would extracurriculars, GPA, and other factors change this? - many schools no longer consider test scores (especially elite colleges). 
Relate: 
As a high school student, I am fairly anxious about college admissions. I've seen a lot of people with really impressive applications who weren't accepted into the schools they wanted. I know someone personally who graduated high school in 2022 with good grades, great test scores, and a year in an exchange program and still got in almost nowhere she applied. 
Headline: 
No Legacy, No Money, No Luck: Bias in College Admissions

raw_comment:
I noticed that when applying for colleges, out of everyone with the exact same test score, legacy students are over twice as likely to be admitted. Furthermore, out of those legacy students, the children whose family has a higher income and makes more money are chosen above the others. A legacy student with a family income in the 99th percentile is 7x more likely to be admitted than the average student with the same test scores. 
I wonder why the colleges are prioritizing financial status when students apply for college. Why has our country’s education system turned away from helping educate students and form capable adults? Why is making more money a bigger priority than equality? I wonder how and if we can fix this inequality. Our country is based off of the idea of equal opportunity, and yet this is anything but equal. 
This affects me as an upcoming senior looking into colleges. It is discouraging knowing that no matter how much I study, other students will still have an unfair advantage. This affects my research in which colleges I might apply to. Knowing I might have a better chance as a legacy student is unfair, but an advantage that some might not help but to exploit. Knowing this data is frustrating, yet it is an advantage to be well informed going into college searches. 
“College Acceptance : the turn from equality and opportunity to moneymaking and legacy”

raw_comment:
I've noticed that, despite college missions departments' claims to the contrary, legacy applicants and parental income have a significant impact on applications. As the information about your parents' making expands, so does the gray region that separates the non-legacy line (bottom and grey) from the legacy line (top and black).
I'm curious as to why the graph exhibits a slight decrease at the 90th percentile of wealth. It makes sense that the admittance rate would rise with wealth, at least based on my educated prediction in the previous question. 
This is relevant to both my town and myself because I know many individuals, including myself, who are always applying to colleges, and there are several prestigious universities in the area that might be prejudiced in their selection process at the moment because of things like legacy status and financial means.
The Reality of How Rigged The College Admission Process Is

raw_comment:
1. This graph represents the likelyness of students with the same test scores but different legacy situations have of getting into an elite school. I noticed that throughout the whole graph, whether rich or poor, legacy students have a better chance of getting into an elite college. I noticed the richer they are, the higher the boost will get as well, the top .1% has 7 times the chance of getting admitted.
2. I wonder why students haven't complained about how unfair it is to get into an elite school. I also wonder just how much money a rich legacy parent must donate so that schools turn their eye and let students in. I wonder how much of a factor test scores make for admissions.
3. This affects my community as a senior as we are looking to get into colleges and have to see the competition we are getting put up against. Rich non legacy students have a lesser chance of getting into the elite schools because they dont fit the criteria of poor diverse students they want to make their school look good or rich legacy students which can throw money at them.
4.  "Is College Rigged"

I notice: The top income bracket has the most likely chance of getting into elite colleges by a large margin Without legacy status, students are much less likely to get into prestigious colleges. Without a legacy boost, it seems that people in the 50-85th income percentile are less likely to get in than lower income brackets. 

I wonder: What are some reasons why the wealthier are more likely to be admitted? Is it because the colleges recognize a chance for a payday? Why is there such a legacy boost? 
Would this trend continue at some less prestigious colleges?

In addition, most in my area are middle class which also diminishes our chances of getting into prestigious programs according to the graph.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice the systemic barriers which keep the rich able to obtain a good education. Those systemic barriers being the legacy boost during college admissions- especially to top selective universities. This graph is appalling by the means which it keeps the less fortunate less fortunate; and, the rich richer via generational wealth and nepotism. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why these colleges still implement legacy boosts during the college admissions process. I wonder what benefit do these universities get by preferring legacy students? Also, how does legacy boost- in addition to affirmative action- completely deplete the middle class’ chance of attending an elite university?

How does this relate to you and your community?
Residing in a rural area I and my fellow peers would most likely be unable to attend an elite university due to the systemic boost of legacy admits- which many legacies attend wealthy private schools. Additionally, we might also not have the different resources for the criterion of admissions at elite universities- which wealthy private schools might have readily available.

raw_comment:
What’s going on in this graph- January 31, 2024

What do you notice?
I notice the systemic barriers which keep the rich able to obtain a good education. Those systemic barriers being the legacy boost during college admissions- especially to top selective universities. This graph is appalling by the means which it keeps the less fortunate less fortunate; and, the rich richer via generational wealth and nepotism. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why these colleges still implement legacy boosts during the college admissions process. I wonder what benefit do these universities get by preferring legacy students? Also, how does legacy boost- in addition to affirmative action- completely deplete the middle class’ chance of attending an elite university?

How does this relate to you and your community?
Residing in a rural area I and my fellow peers would most likely be unable to attend an elite university due to the systemic boost of legacy admits- which many legacies attend wealthy private schools. Additionally, we might also not have the different resources for the criterion of admissions at elite universities- which wealthy private schools might have readily available. 

Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Systemic barriers captivating colleges: Legacies leading admission

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

The trends for legacy and standard applicants almost mirror each other, however, legacy admissions remain higher throughout the whole graph. Also, as income increases, the admission rate increases. My guess is they would like to fuel donations to the school by admitting highly wealthy individuals.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why there is a tiny dip in the graph around the 90th percentile of wealth. You would expect, at least with my guess in the last question, that the admission rate should increase for more wealth, which is generally true. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

My biggest community around me is my classmates. As we are approaching senior year, the college application process is less than a year away. While it may not contribute any useful information to my applications, it highlights the inequalities in the admissions process. Especially when considering elite colleges such as the ones polled, it alters my perspective of the identity of the university. While presenting itself as a prestigious and elite school, it looks as if all they want is your money.

raw_comment:
- I notice that legacy applicants always have a higher chance of being accepted, no matter how rich or poor. Also, for non-legacy applicants, the ranking with the second highest chance of being accepted is 30th, and the lowest is between 80 and 90, which shows that it's not a perfectly direct correlation between how rich you are and how likely you are to get into the school. However, for legacy applicants, the line is more extreme and favors richer students more.
- I wonder how this data was collected and why both lines have a tiny peak right before they get really steep. Additionally, I wonder if the problem would be solved by colleges not having access to parents' income information or whether the applicant is a legacy. The latter would be harder to accomplish, but it seems like withholding the info about money would be relatively easy.
- This relates to my community because I interact with both people who might be legacy applicants and people who might be the first in their family to go to college. The fact that these people would have different chances of getting into an elite college despite having the same test scores is truly frustrating and unfair.  
- My headline is "Affluent Legacy Applicants Receive Extreme Advantages in Elite College Admissions"

raw_comment:
1. I notice how non-legacy applicants from the 10th to 65th percent have a 2x advantage of being accepted in the universities compared to non-legacy applicants from the 65th to 90th. The graph decreases from the 65th to 90th percent income applicants, explaining how richer students are disadvantaged in college acceptance even with the same test scores. After the 90th to the 99th percent, acceptance significantly increases to approximately 2.5 times more.

For legacy applicants, the average admissions rate on the poor side begins at 2.5x. Unlike the non-legacy students, the chance of being accepted as a legacy student increases from 3x to 3.5x after 50 percent. A similar outstanding increase at the 99th percentile is also illustrated, reaching 7x the likelihood of being admitted!

2. I wonder why the two lines went in opposite directions after reaching the 50th percent of income. Why did the legacy applicants have an advantage while the non-legacy applicants had a disadvantage after 50? Have colleges made an effort to change this system of discrimination since 2015? I also wonder if the families in the 99th percentile are admitted for the funding they can offer to the school.

3. This article relates to me because when I apply to universities, being a legacy or non-legacy student for specific schools and my parents' income would significantly affect my admissions.

4. Are you disadvantaged in being accepted into some of the most prestigious universities in the United States?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
In general, rich and legacy applicants are much more likely to be accepted than poorer and/or non-legacy applicants. The acceptance rate for legacy students generally increases the wealthier the family, while the acceptance rate for non-legacy students curves down before spiking. Both types of students acceptance rates spike at the 99.9th income rank.

What do you wonder?
At around the 85th income rank, the admission likeliness for non-legacy students drops below the average admissions rate. I wonder why it drops below at that particular income rank, and not the less-wealthy applicants - could financial aid have something to do with it?

How does this relate to you and your community? 
This relates to me because I'll be applying to college pretty soon, and it's important to know the underlying discrimination of the college admissions process that only continues to grow more relevant.

The Inequality in "Equally-Qualified" Students

What do you notice?

raw_comment:
I noticed that students with parents who have a higher income are more likely to be accepted. While the bottom 50% are about 3x as likely to be accepted, while it climbs quite tremendously in the top 50%. It escalates to the summit where the top 0.1% are 7x more likely to be admitted. I also noticed that without a legacy boost, the top 0.1% has about the same chance to get in as the bottom 10% with a legacy boost. I wonder if this happens because kids with wealthier parents have more money for better education. I also wonder if it has to do with dropping out because of mental illness which can be more common in poorer accommodations. This relates to me and my community because while I go to a school that offers scholarships and is welcoming no matter how wealthy the family is, I know many people don't live like that. Many students get bullied for how much or little money they have. This graph shows the bias in our community toward the wealthy, often because they are able to afford a better education. While people may think that that's fair, it's not really because the parents of these children likely work just as long if not longer than the top 0.1%. The difference is that the top 0.1% was able to make a money harvesting company that the lower class people may not have been able to do because of the bias in society. To sum up, we have a bias in our community because of poverty status

raw_comment:
When I look at the chart for a student with no legacy only, it looks like colleges are trying to “fix” income inequality, except perhaps at the top. A parent-income between 50% and 85% seems to work against the student, and the chance of admission without legacy is exceptionally low. 

I wonder why the legacy boost also dips around the 85% percentile and if donations to colleges increase as parents' income exceeds the 85% mark.

I also wonder what the exact student numbers of legacy vs. non-legacy are for every parent-income number. If legacy is a relatively small number of students, it may be justified for colleges to give this boost to a few ex-students who donated to or otherwise helped their college.

Headline: The Multi-Generational Benefit of an Ivy League Education.

(And the resulting stress to "break in"!)

raw_comment:
Notice: I notice that the graph's scale on the x axis isn’t consistent. It is scaled in a way to make it seem like there is more changing than there really is. The graph’s y axis scale seems more consistent and equally spaced out. Legacy applicants are more likely to be accepted into an Ivy League school than the average admission rate of those students who are not legacy applicants. If their parent’s income rank is higher, there are more students accepted into Ivy League schools in general, but much more for legacy applicants.  

Wonder: I wonder why they felt the need to skew the data on the x axis? What benefit does it really do to encourage the idea that legacy applicants have a more likely chance of being admitted into an Ivy League school?

Relate: This data is applicable and similar to other tiers of colleges as well. Numerous college admissions request essays, and the college may be more likely to accept a legacy applicant than one whose parents either went to another institution or didn’t go to college at all. 

Headline: Legacy Student Advantages in Admissions

raw_comment:
Noticed: The chart is carefully crafted to support a kneejerk reaction that rich legacy applicants are getting admitted at the expense of poor applicants. Looking closer, I notice non-legacy applicants below the 40th income percentile have about 1.75 x the average non-legacy admissions rate. These applicants will likely need a lot of financial aid, due to the bloated cost of college. So the colleges accept a larger proportion of legacy applicants, particularly at the higher income levels. The colleges know that statistically, these applicants’ families will donate large amounts, that can be redistributed down to the 40th percentile and below. Legacy admission advantage and lower-income admissions advantage are the yin and yang of college admissions. At first glance, colleges appear to be acting as Robin Hoods, taking from the rich and giving to the poor. But looking deeper, they are really acting as Grifters – Bloating up their staff and salaries, then stealing from the rich to give to the poor, then demanding the poor turn the money over to – the colleges’ bloated staff and salaries!
It's disappointing but not surprising that The NY Times, which sees victimhood everywhere, cannot bring itself to delve deeper into this to provide a comprehensive, fair analysis.
